question: The approximate radii of hydrogen atom is:
solution:
The correct answer is __**10⁻¹⁰ m**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **radius of a hydrogen atom** is approximately **10⁻¹⁰ meters**. In the field of atomic physics, this specific length scale is also known as **1 Angstrom (Å)**.
 
• More precisely, the **Bohr radius**, which represents the most probable distance between the nucleus and the electron in a **hydrogen atom** in its **ground state**, is calculated to be **0.529 × 10⁻¹⁰ m** (or **0.529 Å**).
 
• The concept of atomic radii was significantly advanced by **Niels Bohr** in the **year 1913** when he proposed his **atomic model**, which successfully explained the spectral lines of **hydrogen**.
 
• A **hydrogen atom** consists of a single **proton** in the **nucleus** and a single **electron** orbiting it. Due to this simple structure, it serves as the fundamental unit for measuring **atomic sizes** in **chemistry** and **physics**.
 
• While the **atom** itself is about **10⁻¹⁰ m** in size, the **nucleus** at its center is significantly smaller, with a **radius** of approximately **10⁻¹⁵ m**, often referred to as a **fermi** or **femtometer**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Units of Measurement:** Atomic dimensions are typically expressed in **nanometers (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m)**, **picometers (1 pm = 10⁻¹² m)**, or **Angstroms (1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m)**. For example, the radius of a **hydrogen atom** is roughly **0.053 nm** or **53 pm**.
 
• **Scale Comparison:** To visualize the **scale**, if an **atom** were expanded to the size of a **football stadium**, the **nucleus** would be roughly the size of a **small marble** placed in the center, highlighting that **atoms** are mostly **empty space**.
 
• **Periodic Table Trends:** The **atomic radius** generally **increases** as you move **down a group** in the **periodic table** due to the addition of **new energy shells**. Conversely, it **decreases** across a **period** from **left to right** because the **effective nuclear charge** increases, pulling **electrons** closer to the **nucleus**.
 
• **Applications:** Understanding the **size of atoms** is crucial in **nanotechnology**, **molecular biology**, and **material science**, as it determines how **atoms** bond and interact to form **molecules**.
 
• **Discovery Context:** **Ernest Rutherford** conducted his famous **gold foil experiment** in **1911**, which led to the discovery of the **nucleus** and established the **nuclear model** of the **atom**, preceding **Bohr’s** refinements.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Atomic Volume:** The **volume** of an **atom** is determined by the **electron cloud**. Since **hydrogen** is the **lightest element** with the **atomic number 1**, it has the **smallest atomic radius** among non-noble gas elements in its neutral state.
 
• **Quantum Mechanics:** In modern **quantum mechanics**, the **electron** does not move in a fixed circular path but exists in an **orbital** or a **probability cloud**. The value **10⁻¹⁰ m** represents the **average distance** or the boundary within which the **electron** is likely to be found.
 
• **Bond Lengths:** The **atomic radius** is often used to calculate **covalent bond lengths**. For a **hydrogen molecule (H₂)**, the **bond length** is approximately **0.74 Å**, which is less than the sum of two **atomic radii** due to **orbital overlap**.
 
• **Scientific Constants:** The **Bohr radius (a₀)** is a **physical constant** used in **Schrödinger's equation** and is approximately **5.29177 × 10⁻¹¹ meters**.
